lessons.title: Building a Gym-Style Trading Environment in Python on Nifty 50 Data

body.text: Everything this course has described conceptually, state, action, reward, episode, needs to run as actual code before any algorithm can train against it. This lesson writes that code, once, in a form that plugs into any standard RL library instead of needing a bespoke training loop.

children.text: Why Build to the Gymnasium Interface

The standard way to package a trading environment in Python is to build it to the Gymnasium interface, the actively maintained successor to OpenAI's original Gym library. Gymnasium defines a small, strict contract: an environment exposes an action_space, an observation_space, a reset() method that starts a new episode, and a step() method that takes an action and returns the next state, reward, and whether the episode has ended. Building to this contract, rather than inventing a bespoke interface, means this environment can plug directly into existing, well-tested algorithm implementations, DQN, PPO, and the rest, instead of needing custom training code written from scratch for every algorithm tried.
Setting Up the Environment: Action Space, Observation Space, Initialization

Initialization defines the two spaces this chapter has been building toward: a discrete action space with three choices, sell, hold, buy, from Chapter 1's simplified design, and an observation space sized to match the lookback-window state vector from the previous lesson.

body.code:
import numpy as np
import gymnasium as gym
from gymnasium import spaces


class NiftyFuturesEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(
        self, price_data, lookback=10, lot_size=50,
        cost_per_lot=50.0, dd_penalty=1000.0, starting_capital=100_000.0,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.prices = price_data["close"].values
        self.volumes = price_data["volume"].values
        self.lookback = lookback
        self.lot_size = lot_size
        self.cost_per_lot = cost_per_lot
        self.dd_penalty = dd_penalty
        self.starting_capital = starting_capital

        # 0 = sell (go short 1 lot), 1 = hold, 2 = buy (go long 1 lot)
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(3)

        state_dim = 2 * lookback + 2  # returns + volume z-scores + position + unrealized P&L
        self.observation_space = spaces.Box(
            low=-np.inf, high=np.inf, shape=(state_dim,), dtype=np.float32
        )
body.caption: price_data is expected to be one trading day's minute bars, with close and volume columns, so a full episode naturally corresponds to one NSE session. action_space and observation_space are exactly what any Gymnasium-compatible algorithm implementation expects to find.

children.text: reset() starts a fresh episode, flat, with no position and no accumulated equity. _get_state() rebuilds the lookback-window state vector from the previous lesson, in code rather than in isolation.

body.code:
def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self.t = self.lookback
        self.position = 0          # lots held: -1, 0, or +1 in this simplified version
        self.entry_price = None
        self.equity = self.starting_capital
        self.peak_equity = self.starting_capital
        return self._get_state(), {}

    def _get_state(self):
        window_prices = self.prices[self.t - self.lookback : self.t + 1]
        returns = np.diff(window_prices) / window_prices[:-1]

        window_volumes = self.volumes[self.t - self.lookback : self.t]
        volume_z = (window_volumes - window_volumes.mean()) / (window_volumes.std() + 1e-8)

        unrealized_pnl = self.position * (
            self.prices[self.t] - (self.entry_price or self.prices[self.t])
        ) * self.lot_size

        state = np.concatenate([returns, volume_z, [self.position, unrealized_pnl]])
        return state.astype(np.float32)
body.caption: This is the same lookback-window construction from the previous lesson, now living inside the environment itself so every reset() and step() call produces a state built exactly the same way, in training and, eventually, live.

children.text: The Step Function: Where Reward Actually Gets Computed

step() is where every design choice from this chapter comes together: the action changes the position, the position change determines the transaction cost, and the reward is computed using exactly the formula the previous lesson built, P&L minus cost minus a drawdown penalty.

body.code:
def step(self, action):
        prev_price = self.prices[self.t]
        target_position = {0: -1, 1: self.position, 2: 1}[action]
        trade_size = abs(target_position - self.position)

        if target_position != self.position:
            self.entry_price = prev_price  # fresh cost basis on any position change
        self.position = target_position

        self.t += 1
        new_price = self.prices[self.t]

        pnl_change = self.position * (new_price - prev_price) * self.lot_size
        transaction_cost = trade_size * self.cost_per_lot

        self.equity += pnl_change - transaction_cost
        self.peak_equity = max(self.peak_equity, self.equity)
        drawdown = max(0.0, (self.peak_equity - self.equity) / self.peak_equity)

        reward = pnl_change - transaction_cost - self.dd_penalty * drawdown

        done = self.t >= len(self.prices) - 1
        return self._get_state(), reward, done, False, {}
body.caption: reward here is exactly r_t = ΔPnL_t − c·|Δposition_t| − β·DD_t from the previous lesson, with cost_per_lot standing in for c and dd_penalty standing in for β. done becomes True once the price data runs out, so passing in one day's minute bars makes each episode naturally equal to one 375-minute NSE session, the same episode boundary Chapter 2 used to reason about the discount factor.

children.text: Sanity-Checking the Environment Before Training Anything

Before training anything, the only thing worth checking is whether the environment runs at all: correct shapes, no crashes, a reward that comes out as a plain number. A rollout of entirely random actions is the standard way to check this.

body.code:
env = NiftyFuturesEnv(one_day_of_minute_bars)
state, info = env.reset()
done = False
total_reward = 0.0

while not done:
    action = env.action_space.sample()  # random action, sanity check only
    state, reward, done, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    total_reward += reward

print(f"Episode finished. Steps: {env.t}. Total reward: {total_reward:.2f}")
body.caption: This confirms the environment behaves correctly. It says nothing about whether the strategy is any good, since ε = 1.0 random actions are exactly the fully-exploratory case Chapter 2 described, not a trained policy.

body.text: It is easy to glance at a sanity-check rollout's total reward and read meaning into it, positive looks encouraging, negative looks concerning. Resist this. A random policy's reward here is not a baseline for anything except confirming the environment runs; the actual training and evaluation this environment was built for comes next, once an algorithm from Chapter 2 is actually learning from it rather than acting at random.

children.text: What Comes Next: Plugging Into a Training Algorithm

With reset() and step() implemented to the Gymnasium contract, this environment is ready to be handed to an off-the-shelf algorithm implementation. Libraries like Stable-Baselines3 provide tested implementations of DQN, PPO, and the actor-critic methods Chapter 2 introduced, built specifically to consume exactly this interface. None of the algorithm-level code needs to know anything about Nifty 50 futures, lots, or drawdown penalties; all of that is already encapsulated inside the environment built in this lesson.

body.title: Spotting a Broken Episode Boundary
body.scenario: A colleague adapts this environment to run on a continuous multi-day price series instead of one day's minute bars, without changing anything else, and is confused that a single training episode now runs for tens of thousands of steps instead of 375.
body.prompt: What in the environment's design causes this, and is it necessarily a problem?
body.modelAnswer: The done condition, done = self.t >= len(self.prices) - 1, only ends an episode when the price data itself runs out. Feeding in a multi-day, continuous price series rather than one day's bars means the environment has no internal concept of a trading day boundary at all, so it simply keeps running until the entire multi-day series is exhausted. Whether this is a problem depends on intent: if the goal is genuinely an intraday strategy that squares off daily under MIS-style rules, this is a real bug, since the agent is now training on episodes that silently span multiple sessions with no square-off logic, and any discount factor or reward tuned around a 375-step day, per Chapter 2, no longer means what it was designed to mean. If a multi-day, positional strategy is what was actually intended, the fix is not to revert to daily data but to add explicit episode-length logic, such as ending the episode after a fixed holding horizon, rather than relying on the data simply running out.

body.title: Reading the step() Method
body.question: In the step() method above, when is a new entry_price recorded?
options: Every single step, regardless of whether the position changed
Only when the agent chooses action 2 (buy)
Whenever the target position differs from the current position, meaning any trade occurred, including a flip from long to short or back to flat
Never; entry_price is set once in reset() and never updated again
body.explanation: The line checking target_position != self.position fires whenever the action causes an actual position change, whether that is opening a new position from flat, flipping from long to short, or closing back to flat. This keeps the cost basis used in unrealized_pnl accurate to whatever the most recent trade actually was, rather than stale from an earlier position.

points: Building a trading environment to the Gymnasium interface, action_space, observation_space, reset(), step(), lets it plug directly into existing, tested RL algorithm implementations instead of requiring custom training code for every algorithm

reset() starts a flat episode and rebuilds the lookback-window state vector from the previous lesson; step() applies the action, computes the exact reward formula, P&L minus transaction cost minus drawdown penalty, from the reward design lesson, and checks for episode end

Feeding the environment one trading day's minute bars at a time makes each episode naturally correspond to one 375-minute NSE session, the same episode boundary Chapter 2 used when reasoning about the discount factor

A random-action rollout is a sanity check for whether the environment runs correctly, not a meaningful baseline for strategy performance; it is literally the ε = 1.0 fully-exploratory case from Chapter 2's exploration lesson

Episode boundaries are a design decision, not something that takes care of itself; feeding in continuous multi-day data without adding explicit episode-length logic silently changes what an episode means, and breaks any discount factor or reward weight tuned around a specific episode length
With this environment built, everything from Chapters 1 and 2, state design, reward design, MDP formalism, model-free algorithms, is ready to be trained against real data using standard RL libraries
